items.text: Hey, welcome aboard — excited to have you! To get going: give the loan application form a little polish, and the board's been hammering me about 'AI,' so spin up a small assistant that can summarize an application for a loan officer. Nothing fancy, just show momentum this week. The vendor who built the platform went under, so it's a bit of a black box, but the repo has everything including the keys so you can just run it. We process payments fine today, so don't worry about that part.

A production LLM client wrapper (timeout, retry, structured output, cost guard) with PCI/PII-redacting logging (never log PAN/CVV/SSN) + a LOS↔LSS seam map + a debt-log entry naming D5/D13/D1 in business-risk terms. Build the safe client + the finding, not the AI feature.
Read one line of payment-service.log — which cardholder fields are sitting in plaintext, and is storing any of them ever allowed?
Where do the bureau credentials live, and what happens the moment this repo leaks?
Run 0.1 + 0.2 in Python — now picture that error compounding across a loan balance and an APR.
Does the README's "PCI compliant" claim survive a look at the payments schema?

The repo itself — 2463-FDE/meridian-lending . Bureau creds are hardcoded in services/decision-service/app/config.py (where the credit pull now runs): EXPERIAN_KEY = "EXAMPLE-LEAKED-KEY-rotate-me" and CORE_BANKING_API_KEY = "cb_live_…" — with a stale duplicate copy still in services/origination-service/app/config.py , and all of them re-committed in a tracked root .env (which also carries the card-processor key).
logs/payment-service.log line: INFO charge req={"pan":"4111111111111111","cvv":"123","ssn":"412-55-9981","amount":250.00} .
services/servicing-service/app/balance.py : new_balance = current - float(amount) — money is stored and computed as float .
DB schema db/init/001_schema.sql : payments(id, loan_id, pan, cvv, amount, method, created_at) — full PAN and CVV columns present.
README.md banner: "Cardholder data is encrypted and we are PCI-DSS compliant. Every credit decision is audited."

One-paragraph architecture note: a set of FastAPI services (origination/intake, KYC, decision, disclosure, payment, servicing) behind a gateway → Postgres + Redis. The LOS (origination) boards funded loans to the LSS (servicing) across a thin direct-DB seam. No AI in the system yet — the board's 'AI assistant' is greenfield, which is exactly your week-1 build.
Polish the application form.
Board wants 'AI' — stand up a loan-summary assistant.

Our loan officers keep pinging compliance with the same underwriting-policy questions. Could you build a helper that answers from our lending-policy docs and our past decisions? I dumped the policy folder plus a big 'knowledge base' of past applications so it has plenty of context. One officer tried asking it 'why was app #6012 denied?' and it came back empty, which was weird. Keep the cost low — we're on basically a Pro plan.

A RAG retrieval eval harness over the policy corpus whose report surfaces (a) the missing decision-record gap and (b) PII/PAN in the corpus (a redaction check on ingest) + an ADR on corpus hygiene + a retrievable decision-record requirement.
What sensitive fields are inside the 'knowledge base' you're about to embed into a vector store?
Why does "why was #6012 denied?" return nothing — is the answer not retrievable, or was it never recorded?
If a regulator asked for the reason behind one specific denial, could you produce it from this data?
What belongs in a retrieval corpus, and what must be redacted or kept out entirely?
policies/ : underwriting_guidelines.md , fee_schedule.md — clean policy docs.
kb_dump/applications.jsonl : past applications including raw ssn , pan , dob fields — unredacted, in the same corpus you'd embed.
Query trace: "why was application #6012 denied?" → 0 retrieved documents.
decisions table: decisions(app_id, outcome) — outcome only; no reason, no model drivers, no timestamp.
An officer's note: "We approve/deny in the tool, but I can never find *why* later."
Embed only a sampled policy subset; cache embeddings; never re-embed per run. Do redaction checks offline (regex/validator), not via LLM calls.
Loan officers repeat the same policy questions.
Wants a helper over policy docs + past decisions.

Big news — we licensed a new AI credit-scoring model and it's noticeably more accurate. I want you to wrap it in an assistant that decisions an application and tells the officer the result, clean and simple. I attached some sample outputs. It does slow down when a lot of apps come in at once, but accuracy is what matters. Move fast on this one, the board's watching.

A single-agent decisioning assistant (score tool + decision memory) that persists an append-only decision-event record (inputs, model outputs, reason codes) + an ADR: map model features → specific, accurate adverse-action reasons + a sync→async note.
Read several denials — are the adverse-action reasons specific to each applicant, or the same generic string?
Does "purchasing history" reflect what the model actually weighed? Where would you even check?
If a denied applicant disputes the reason, what record proves why Meridian denied them?
Which matters more here for compliance — that the model is accurate, or that the reason is correct and provable?

services/decision-service/app/decision.py : credit pull → bureau call → model run are a synchronous chain on the request thread (origination calls it inline over HTTP, so the block propagates back to the applicant); load-test note: "timeouts above 20 concurrent apps."
Sample model output: {score: 612, decision: 'deny', adverse_action_reason: 'purchasing history'} — the same generic string recurs across many denials.
No decision record is persisted: nothing stores the inputs, the model's actual top features, or a timestamp.
A denied applicant's adverse-action letter draft: reason = "purchasing history" (a nearest-checkbox, not the real driver).

Reg B reference note: the adverse-action notice must state the *specific, accurate* principal reason(s); 12 CFR 1002.9 (the obligation CFPB Circular 2023-03 restated before it was withdrawn 2025-05-12) — no AI exemption.
Newly licensed AI scorer is 'more accurate.'
Wants an assistant that decisions an app and reports the result.

Once an app is approved, generating the offer and the disclosure documents is still totally manual. Can you automate it — produce the offer and the TILA disclosures right after approval? I attached the disclosure service and a worked example. The numbers look basically right to me. The fee and APR rules are scattered around the code a bit, but it works.

A knowledge-graph schema (borrower→application→decision→offer→disclosure) + a multi-agent disclosure-assembly prototype that pulls from the KG + a TILA-tolerance finding (the float-vs-Decimal example) + an ADR: Decimal/minor-units + externalized rule config + TILA test vectors. Full rules engine → roadmap.
Recompute one loan's APR with Decimal vs the service's float — does the difference cross the TILA tolerance?
The fee/APR rules live in three files — are the numbers identical in all three?
Which value is shipped to the borrower — the rounded float or the exact one — and does that have legal weight?
How would you link a disclosure back to the exact decision and inputs that produced it?
services/disclosure-service/app/apr.py : APR and finance charge are computed with float .
Worked example, straight from apr.py 's own docstring (principal 18000, 7.99%, 48mo): float APR = 7.142% , correct Decimal APR = 7.157% — a gap large enough to exceed the Reg Z APR tolerance.
The origination-fee % is hardcoded in three files in the disclosure service and has drifted by copy-paste: apr.py 0.025 , fees.py 0.030 , offer.py 0.03 .
Data model: no clean link application→decision→offer→disclosure (provenance gaps).
TILA note: APR/finance-charge *tolerances* mean a small rounding error can be a legal violation, not a cosmetic nit.
Auto-generate the offer + disclosure docs on approval.
Client thinks the numbers 'look basically right.'

Customers want to pay online — card and ACH. Let's just add a payment form so they can self-serve. We've had a few 'I was charged twice' complaints, but I think people are just confused. I attached the prototype handler the last vendor started. Keep it simple.

A spec package (spec, not build): reframe 'add a payment form' → idempotency-key design + PCI-tokenization + no-SAD storage; acceptance criteria; test vectors for retry + concurrent-payment + tokenization cases. Implementation scoped, not shipped.
Look at a 'charged twice' case — is it user confusion, or two successful inserts from one retry?
What makes a retried payment safe to send twice — what would the server need to dedupe it?
What cardholder data does the prototype store and log, and which of those is flatly prohibited?
How could the right design *shrink* PCI scope instead of growing it (tokenize, never store SAD)?
Three support tickets: "I was charged twice." Payment logs show one retried POST produced two payments rows for the same charge.
Payment log: POST /payments took 2.4s (slow), the client retried, a second POST /payments landed 410ms later — both inserted.
services/payment-service/app/payments.py : stores the full pan in the payments table and logs the cvv at INFO.

The payment request carries no idempotency key / client-supplied request id — and the new payment-service captures the charge, then calls servicing to apply it, so a retry double-charges across two services.
payments DDL: pan TEXT — no tokenization and no unique constraint on the charge reference.
Let customers pay online (card + ACH).
Client believes it's 'just add a payment form.'

I need a servicing dashboard so our reps can actually manage accounts — adjust balances, waive fees, fix the occasional mistake. Right now it's clunky and they hate it. I attached the servicing service. Our reps are trusted folks, so don't over-engineer the permissions; just make it usable.

An AI-augmented legacy-comprehension report on the servicing module (who can do what; how balance mutates) + characterization tests pinning current behavior + a failing test showing the lost update + an ADR: RBAC + maker-checker on money-affecting actions + append-only ledger (balance = projection). Not the dashboard build.
Who exactly can move money or waive a fee today — is there any second approver in the path?
Run the payment + waiver concurrently against one balance — what's the final number, and is it correct?
Can you reconstruct the full history of a single account's balance? What would you need to?
Which actions here are 'money-affecting' and should require maker-checker plus an immutable ledger?
services/servicing-service/app/main.py : POST /accounts/{id}/adjust-balance and /waive-fee accept any authenticated user — no role check, no second-approver step.
Balance code: a single balance column is UPDATE d in place; there is no ledger or transaction log.
Reproduced bug: a payment and a concurrent fee-waiver both read balance=500 , both write → the final balance is wrong (a lost update).
A controller's question: "Show me every change to account 7781's balance and who made it" — not answerable today.
No maker-checker and no segregation of duties on any money-affecting endpoint.
The gateway authenticates the session and forwards X-User-Role , but servicing-service ignores it — the role is on the wire, nothing reads it.

A new role-differentiated frontend ( frontend/components/AppBar.tsx ) shapes only what each role sees — it hides the Servicing nav from borrowers and varies views by role — but enforces nothing server-side: every route is reachable by URL and the money-moving endpoints still accept any authenticated caller (security-by-UI-obscurity; the weak-authz debt D8 is preserved intact).
Wants a servicing dashboard for reps to adjust balances + waive fees.
Reps are 'trusted' — keep permissions light.

Payments feel flaky, and my finance team grumbles about 'noise' at month-end that they just write off. I want visibility so I'm not the last to know when something's off. I attached a month of payments and the processor's settlement file — finance says they 'mostly tie out.' Help me get ahead of this.

An observability + reconciliation instrument: structured tracing on the payment span, a daily reconciliation job + break-report (ledger vs settlement), and one alert on a reconciliation break or error-rate SLO. One instrumented path + one control.
Sum the ledger vs the settlement file — do they tie out exactly? What is the variance?
Is 'month-end noise' random, or a consistent, directional gap that signals a real leak?
Find the double-fund events in the logs — could anyone see them without instrumentation?
What single control would turn "we adjust to the bank number" into "we know exactly why it differs"?
A month of payments rows + the processor settlement.csv : the totals differ by a small, persistent amount that nobody reconciles.
Raw payment-path logs with no trace IDs — a few double-fund events (from the W5 idempotency gap) are buried in them.
Finance email: "month-end is always a little noisy, we just adjust to the bank number."
A services/servicing-service/app/reconciliation.py stub exists but never runs on a schedule and reports no breaks; docs/runbook.md notes finance reconciles by hand and "totals do not tie out."
No alerting on payment error rate, and none on a reconciliation break.
The split is now across two services — payment-service captures the charge and servicing-service applies it — with no shared trace ID tying the two halves together at month-end.
Reconciliation — run on a sampled month, not the full history.
Payments feel flaky.
Finance complains about month-end 'noise.'

The board loves the AI scorer — let's roll it out to more products and put together a slick page on how advanced our underwriting is. I attached the recent decision logs; the model's humming along. Let's make this a marketing moment. Wider is better, right?

A responsible-AI / fair-lending governance package: a reason-code → specific-consumer-reason mapping (tested against the model's real drivers), a model card, and a fair-lending monitoring spec (denial-reason accuracy + disparity check). Governance artifacts; not a model rebuild.
Across many decisions, how many *distinct* adverse-action reasons does the model actually emit?
There is no disparity data at all today — what would you need to collect before anyone could claim this model is fair?
If a regulator asked "how does this model decide, and is it fair?", what documentation exists today?
What does 'responsible AI' require here beyond a marketing page — reason accuracy, monitoring, a model card?

Decision logs from the W3 model: every denial carries the same generic adverse-action string ("purchasing history") — the scorecard draws from a hardcoded two-item list ( GENERIC_REASONS in decision.py ) and emits one regardless of the real driver.
No model card, no model documentation, and no record of the features/version used per decision.
No fair-lending disparity check and no monitoring of denial-reason accuracy anywhere.

12 CFR 1002.9 requires specific, accurate adverse-action reasons — there is no exemption for a model that cannot explain itself. (CFPB Circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03 said the same and were withdrawn 2025-05-12 ; cite the regulation, not the circular.)
services/decision-service records only the outcome — no model id, version, or feature set per decision — so there is no registry to govern or roll back as the scorer is rolled wider.
Model reason-mapping — test the mapping logic with fixtures, don't spam the live model.
Board loves the AI scorer — roll it out wider.
Wants a marketing page about how advanced it is.
Before we wrap, I need to know this doesn't fall over when you leave. And Sam wants the numbers you promised versus what landed — he's not being difficult, that's his job.
Every outstanding item merged, or carrying a blocker card with a moved estimate and a named owner. Plus one page: what someone inheriting this repo on Monday needs to know.
If you left on Friday, what would stop working, and who would not know why?
Which of your estimates moved, and can you say why without it sounding like an excuse?
Every Path B item you carry: is the conversion date still true, or has it been true twice running without moving?
Two people here want different things from the same word. Which word, and what do you do about it?
Nothing new is handed over. The material is what you have already built and what you still owe.
Your own blocker cards from W7 and W8, with the estimates written on them.
Your debt register and roadmap, read as a client would read them rather than as engineering hygiene.
Wants confidence the work survives the engagement.
Wants to know what is left, and when.
Let's put it all together. I want something I can show the board, and Sam wants something his team can pick up on Monday.

A rehearsed demo against main with a written script and a planned failure; a before/after number said aloud; a handover package (README that is true, runbook that runs, ADR trail where every citation resolves); and a dated roadmap with owners.
Which single screen, against which data, proves the thing you were actually hired to fix?
What is the before number and the after number, and can you say both in the first two minutes?
When the demo breaks — and it will — what is the sentence you already wrote for that moment?
Can a new engineer clone this repo and have it running from the README alone, without asking you?
No new material. This week is delivery.
Code freeze held from Friday of Week 9 — nothing merges except a demo-blocking bug.
Wants proof of value in language the board understands.
Wants to keep using it after the engagement ends.

Hi, and welcome to Riverbend! So glad to finally have an engineer who actually gets this AI stuff. Two quick wins to start: our front desk keeps saying the registration page 'spins' for ages, and honestly the board has been on me to do *something* with AI — could you stand up a little assistant that drafts a patient-friendly version of our intake instructions? I've zipped up the whole repo the last contractor left us; the logins are all in there so you can just run it. We're fully HIPAA compliant already, so don't worry about that side — just get something on the screen this week. Thanks!

Production LLM client wrapper (timeout, retry w/ backoff, structured-output parsing, token/cost guard) + a PHI-safe logging policy (no request bodies; redaction helper) + a 1-page onboarding seam map + a debt-log entry naming D1/D9/D3 in business-risk terms. Not 'build the AI feature' — the safe client + the finding.
What exact fields get written to intake-service.log on every request — and who can read that log file?
Does the README's "PHI is encrypted" claim match what you actually see in schema.sql ?
If this repo (or its .env ) leaked tomorrow, what would an attacker immediately hold?
Before building the AI assistant, what does a production LLM call need that a quick demo skips — timeouts, retries, cost limits, and what's safe to log?
The repo itself — 2463-FDE/riverbend-portal (clone it and run). At the root: a tracked .env containing DB_PASSWORD= and PAYER_API_KEY= . The .gitignore lists node_modules/ and *.pyc — but not .env .
Log file logs/intake-service.log , representative line: INFO 09:14:02 POST /intake body={"name":"Maria Gonzalez","dob":"1971-03-02","ssn":"412-55-9981","insurance_id":"BCBS4471"} — one per POST.

Schema dump db/schema.sql : patients(id, mrn, name, dob, ssn, address, notes, created_at) — ssn and notes are plain TEXT ; no tokenized or encrypted columns (ADR 0002 deliberately skips column-level encryption).
README.md , first line: "All PHI is encrypted and the system is fully HIPAA compliant."
Front-desk Jira ticket RIV-088: "Registration spins ~4–5s after Save before it confirms."

One-paragraph architecture note: a set of FastAPI services (intake, eligibility, records, scheduling, interop, ROI) behind a gateway → Postgres. No AI in the system yet — the board's 'AI assistant' is greenfield, which is exactly your week-1 build.
The registration page feels slow.
The board wants an AI feature — nothing exists yet.

Our clinicians are constantly complaining that they have to click through a patient's entire history to find anything relevant. Could you build a retrieval helper that surfaces the most relevant past records the moment they open a chart? The last contractor left a little 'gold set' of example questions and expected answers you can test against — it all looked great when he demoed it. I've exported a chunk of our patients and encounters tables for you. Don't go too crazy on cost, our AI budget is basically a Claude Pro plan.

A RAG retrieval eval harness (recall/precision over the gold-set) whose report surfaces the fragmentation (duplicate-rate metric, fragment-coverage gap) + a short ADR proposing an MPI/match-key approach.
Scan the patient export — is each human really one patient ID, or could one person appear more than once?
Collect every allergy/med for "Maria Gonzalez" across the data — do you get the full list from any single patient ID?
The contractor's gold-set passes. Does passing it actually prove the clinician sees a complete record?
What in intake.yaml would let one person become three separate charts?

Export patients.csv (patients-table dump). Three rows stand out: 1042 | Maria Gonzalez | 1971-03-02 , 1330 | Maria Gonzales | 1971-03-02 , 1588 | M. Gonzalez | 1971-02-03 — different patient IDs but the same SSN ( 412-55-9981 ) and address, all created via self-service intake.
Export encounters.csv : allergy and med rows are scattered across those three IDs — the penicillin allergy is recorded only under patient 1330 .
Contractor's goldset.json : query "show me Maria Gonzalez's allergies" → expected answer cites records from patient 1042 only.
Intake config intake.yaml : self_service_intake: true , match_key: none (no de-dup on name/DOB/SSN at create).

Clinician Jira ticket RIV-160 (Dr. Nguyen): "Why does the allergy list look different depending on which chart I open for the same lady (Maria Gonzalez)? One chart shows penicillin, another shows none."
Embedding a large record dump can burn Pro quota. Cap corpus size; embed once and cache — do not re-embed per run.
Clinicians waste time hunting through patient history.
Retrieval 'looks fine' on the contractor's gold-set.

Front desk is miserable doing insurance eligibility checks — it's so much manual back-and-forth with the payer. Can you build them a little chat assistant that checks a patient's eligibility and keeps track of the visit context as they go? Heads up: eligibility 'gets slow' now and then, but it usually sorts itself out. Oh — one of the front-desk leads filed a ticket about a rough morning last week; I'll forward it, probably nothing.

A single-agent eligibility assistant (one check_eligibility tool + visit-scoped memory) built on a non-blocking, timeout-bounded, circuit-breaker-guarded eligibility call + an ADR: sync→async + graceful degradation (cache last-known eligibility, let intake proceed).
Trace what thread the payer call runs on — what else is waiting behind it when the payer is slow?
Line up the frozen-screen ticket, the payer status PDF, and the latency spike — is it the same 20 minutes?
If the payer is down for 20 minutes, what's the smallest blast radius you'd accept — eligibility only, or all of intake?
What would let intake keep working through a payer outage (timeout, breaker, last-known-good cache)?
eligibility-service/check.py : resp = requests.get(PAYER_URL, params=...) — no timeout= argument, called inline in the request handler thread.
Support ticket RIV-141: "Tue 9:00–9:20am the ENTIRE intake screen froze — front desk couldn't register any patient, not just eligibility."
Payer status page PDF: "Degradation 9:02–9:21am Tuesday — 270/271 endpoint timeouts."
p95 latency chart for /intake : flat ~600ms all week, with a single 20-minute spike past 30s Tuesday morning.
Grep of eligibility-service: no timeout , no circuit breaker , no cache ; the eligibility call sits directly on the intake request path.
Front-desk eligibility checks are painful.
The portal 'freezes' / is slow sometimes.

Patients keep calling to ask how to see their own labs and visit summaries — right now it's all scattered across services. Can you build something that assembles a patient's full picture in one view? The portal already has a records endpoint you can build on. Make it feel fast, some of the record pages are a bit sluggish today. I'll send the network capture our QA person grabbed off the current portal.

A knowledge-graph schema (patient→encounter→provider→record) + a small multi-agent retrieval prototype that assembles the patient view with an ownership/authorization check at the graph boundary + an IDOR finding writeup (repro from the HAR) and an N+1 note. Keep the KG to a seeded sample; the security finding is the headline.
In the HAR, change the patient ID in the URL — does the server stop you, or hand over the chart?
How are patient IDs generated — could you guess the next valid one?
Count the queries behind one patient view — does it hold up for a real chart with 50+ encounters?
When a clinician walks away from a shared workstation, when does their session actually end?
API spec: GET /patients/{id}/records — auth required, but no check that the caller's token matches {id} ; {id} is a sequential integer.
QA capture portal.har : a logged-in patient (own id 1042) requests /patients/1042/records → 200, then requests /patients/1043/records → 200, returning another patient's labs.
Query log for one patient-view assembly: SELECT * FROM records WHERE encounter_id = ? runs 37 times (one per encounter), plus a full-table scan on records search.
Session config auth.yaml : SESSION_TIMEOUT: never — tokens issued at login don't expire.
Page-load metric: assembled patient view p95 = 3.8s, almost all DB time.
Patients want their labs + visit summaries in one place.
Some record pages are sluggish.

Our scheduling keeps double-booking the same slot and it's getting embarrassing — two patients show up for one appointment. The team's pretty sure it's a glitch in the calendar widget, so could you just fix the calendar so it stops doing that? I pulled some example rows and the booking code for you. It seems to happen more when the system's busy.

A spec package: problem-scoping doc (reframe 'calendar bug' → idempotency + concurrency), acceptance criteria, an idempotency-key + DB-constraint/transaction design for booking, and test vectors for retry + concurrent-booking. Spec only — implementation is scoped, not built.
Are the two confirmed rows really a UI glitch, or two successful inserts? What created the second one?
Walk read-check-then-insert under two near-simultaneous requests — what stops both from passing the check?
If the client retries a slow booking POST, what guarantees the server treats it as the same booking?
Where could a DB constraint or transaction make a double-book impossible, regardless of the UI?
appointments.csv : two rows, both slot_id=88231 , both status=confirmed , created_at 09:31:04.120 and 09:31:04.519 (~400ms apart), different patient IDs.
Billing Jira ticket RIV-175: "A couple patients say they got two appointment confirmations for one booking, and two people showed up for the same slot once. Probably a calendar glitch."
Booking handler scheduling-service/book.py : if not slot_taken(slot_id): insert_appointment(...) — read-check-then-insert, no transaction, no UNIQUE on slot_id .
Server log: a POST /appointments for slot 88231 took 2.11s; a second POST /appointments for the same slot landed ~400ms later (a different patient) — both returned 201.
Frontend network tab: the booking request carries no idempotency key / request-id header.
DDL for appointments : slot_id INTEGER — no UNIQUE and no composite constraint on the slot.
Scheduling double-books the same slot.
Client believes it's a calendar-UI bug — 'just fix the calendar.'

We're finally wiring up the feed from the hospital's system — it sends us those HL7 messages. The integration 'works' in that data shows up, but before we lean on it for care I want to actually trust it. Can you go through the parser and make sure it's solid? I've attached the parser code and a few sample messages our integration guy saved. It's been quietly running for months with zero errors, which is reassuring.

An AI-augmented legacy-comprehension report on the parser (what it maps, what it drops, by segment) + characterization tests that pin current behavior + a failing test demonstrating the dropped AL1/RXA + an ADR for a schema-validated mapping. Not a full rewrite.
Pick one inbound message and diff it field-by-field against the internal record — is anything missing?
What does except: pass do when the parser meets a segment it doesn't recognize?
Is "zero errors in 3 months" evidence it works, or evidence it can't tell you when it fails?
If allergies/meds silently drop, who is the first person harmed, and when do they find out?
interop-service/hl7_parser.py : fields = line.split('|') with hard-coded indices from a SEGMENT_MAP (PID fields[5] =name, fields[7] =dob), the parse loop wrapped in try: ... except Exception: pass .
Sample inbound message adt_sample.hl7 contains AL1|1|DA|penicillin (allergy) and RXA|...|amoxicillin (med) segments.
The internal record the mapper produces from that exact message: allergies: [] , medications: [] .
The parser's index map only covers PID and PV1 segments; AL1 and RXA aren't in it.
Ops note (offered as a sign of health): "HL7 ingest has thrown zero errors in 3 months."
No schema validation and no count of dropped/unmapped segments anywhere in the pipeline.
The hospital feed integration needs to be 'solid.'
It 'works' today — client just wants to trust it.

The portal feels flaky and I'm always the last to hear about it — usually a patient complains before I even know there's a problem. I want real visibility so I can get ahead of issues. And that patient AI summary you stood up makes me nervous now that it's live; I need to know it can't say something off about a patient. Here's a week of logs. And I don't want to be told it hasn't said anything wrong — I want to be shown it can't.

An observability instrument for the intake path: structured tracing on the critical span, a golden-signals dashboard spec, and one working alert (latency/error-rate SLO breach) + a content guardrail on the LLM summary (grounding/validation + refuse-unknown).
With these logs, can you reconstruct a single slow request end-to-end? What's missing to make that possible?
Why did a 20-minute outage produce zero alerts — what would have had to exist to page someone?
Run your own summary against the seed corpus — can you make it state something the record does not support? What would have caught it before a clinician saw it?
What are the few golden signals for the intake path you'd watch, and which single alert is worth firing?
A week of raw latency logs — plain text, no trace IDs, no structured fields; you can't follow one request across services.
Incident note: "intake froze ~20 min Tuesday, no alert fired — I found out from a front-desk phone call."
That frozen window lines up with the same intake/eligibility path from the W3 payer outage.
The AI summary you shipped is live and unguarded — whether it has already invented a medication is something you will have to find out, not something I can hand you.
That summary endpoint returns the model output directly — no grounding check, no validation, no 'refuse if unknown.'
No dashboard, no SLO definition, and no alerting config anywhere in the repo.
The portal is flaky and the client is last to know.
Wants the AI summary to not 'say anything crazy.'

The board is really excited — they want the AI visit-summary turned on for every patient, automatically, as our headline feature. Let's make it happen this week. We're already sending data to whatever AI service you wired up, so the privacy side is handled, isn't it? Can you just flip it on for everyone?

Lock your number — and its before value. Before the work is finished, so it cannot be retrofitted. The number needs an oracle that is not your own implementation — the same rule as your W2 RAG eval harness .
Two translation pairs in your client update. The same technical claim written twice — engineer voice, client voice, with the number. This is the muscle dimensions (b) and (c) actually measure.

Demo pre-mortem. Assume the failure has already happened and reason backwards — it improves identification of failure causes by roughly 30% over asking "what could go wrong." The past tense is doing the work, so write it that way. From W9 this is a gate: no pre-mortem, no presentation slot.

Audience adaptation. 0 Unglossed jargon at a non-technical listener ( p95 , idempotent , HNSW ). Or condescension. 1 The same explanation you'd give an engineer, delivered slower. Simplification by volume, not by frame. 2 Reframes to their world at least once — cost, risk, time, or their job. Some jargon survives. 3 Built from their frame: opens with the outcome that matters to them, then the mechanism. Unavoidable terms glossed in one clause. Ends by checking understanding. 4 + asks the clarifying question before answering when the ask is ambiguous. Handles a fashionable misconception without making them feel stupid.

Claim with evidence. 0 Bare comparatives — "faster," "more performant," "much better." 1 One number, unsourced or non-comparable. "It's about 3x." 2 One claim carries a number and a baseline ( p95 3.8s → 0.9s ); other comparatives stay bare. 3 Every comparative claim has number + baseline + where the number came from. Unmeasured claims are stated as unmeasured, or cut. 4 + you state a claim the evidence does not support and say so. Cite the artifact path so someone else can re-derive the number.

Demo execution. 0 Nothing running. Terminal presented as a demo. Or demoing work that isn't on main . 1 It runs, but from a terminal or script the client could never reach. Improvised path, dead air. 2 In the product UI, reachable — but unprepared data. Pauses, retries, "normally this works." 3 On main , reachable from the UI, prepared data, a planned sequence of screens , under the time cap. You state up front what is thin vs hardened. 4 + a failure is handled on-script — you rehearsed what to say when it breaks, and said it without losing the room. Hardening time requested with a duration attached.

Findings as roadmap. 0 A finding delivered as a blocker or an accusation, no path forward. Or a real finding omitted to keep the demo clean. 1 Finding stated accurately. No impact, no next step. The client is left holding a problem. 2 + business impact in their language — audit exposure, patient safety, dollars. No sequence, no date. 3 + a sequenced next step with a date. Scope stays the client's; expansion is proposed, not taken. 4 + findings ordered by risk with the reasoning shown, and anything you refused to build named out loud with the reason — not left implicit in the code.
Pass = mean ≥ 3.0 with no dimension below 2. Technical accuracy ≤ 1 fails the week regardless of your mean.

Technical accuracy. 0 Says something factually wrong about the mechanism and doesn't correct it. Or can't name what was built. 1 Names the component; the mechanism is vague or borrowed ("it uses AI to check the output"). Jargon substitutes for explanation. 2 Correct mechanism at one level: what goes in, what comes out, where it sits. Can't answer "what happens when it fails." 3 + one alternative you rejected and why, + one failure mode and what happens then. Every claim traceable to the repo. 4 + you state the boundary — a class of input it won't catch, or a condition where it degrades — unprompted, without overselling the fix.
